flashcards.q: What are the three distinct guarantees provided by refresh, flush, and merge?
flashcards.a: Refresh = visibility (search can see the document, default every 1s). Flush = durability (segments fsync'd to disk, translog cleared). Merge = efficiency (fewer segments to search, deleted docs reclaimed). They are three different things, not synonyms.

flashcards.q: Why isn't a document searchable the instant it's indexed?
flashcards.a: It's added to an in-memory buffer and the translog, but only becomes searchable after a refresh (default interval 1s) turns the buffer into a new immutable Lucene segment. This is what 'near-real-time' means precisely.

flashcards.q: A term query for the exact phrase 'Redis Cluster' against a text-mapped field returns nothing. Why?
flashcards.a: The text field is analyzed at index time into separate lowercased tokens ('redis', 'cluster'), not the raw phrase. A term query compares the raw input against those individual tokens, so a multi-token phrase never matches. Fix: use a keyword field/sub-field for exact match.

flashcards.q: What's the first knob to turn under heavy bulk-indexing load, and what does it trade off?
flashcards.a: Raise (or disable, -1) refresh_interval. Fewer, larger segments get created per unit time, reducing merge pressure and indexing overhead, at the cost of increased search-visibility latency.

flashcards.q: What is the default scoring function in Elasticsearch, and what two parameters define it?
flashcards.a: BM25 (default since Lucene 6 / ES 5, 2016, replacing TF-IDF). k1 (default 1.2) controls term-frequency saturation; b (default 0.75) controls document-length normalization.

flashcards.q: What does BM25's term-frequency saturation (k1) fix relative to plain TF-IDF?
flashcards.a: TF-IDF scales score linearly with term frequency with no cap; BM25's k1 makes repeated occurrences of a term contribute diminishing returns instead of scaling forever.

flashcards.q: What's the difference between a query clause and a filter clause?
flashcards.a: A query clause contributes to the relevance score. A filter clause (bool.filter/must_not) is a yes/no check with no scoring contribution, and is cacheable since the answer doesn't depend on scoring math -- generally cheaper to execute.

flashcards.q: What causes oversharding and what's its observable symptom?
flashcards.a: Provisioning far more shards than data volume/node count justify -- each shard carries real per-shard memory and cluster-state overhead. Symptom: heap usage climbs and query/indexing latency degrades with no correlation to actual data growth, plus slow cluster-state updates.

flashcards.q: What's the commonly recommended shard size range, and the fix for an already-oversharded cluster?
flashcards.a: Roughly 10-50GB per shard. Fix an oversharded cluster by reindexing into fewer, larger shards (or _shrink for read-only indices) -- you can't just reduce a live index's primary shard count in place.

flashcards.q: Why does from/size pagination get slow and error past 10,000 results, and what replaces it?
flashcards.a: Each shard must compute and sort from+size results before the coordinator merges/re-sorts across shards, so cost grows with depth; index.max_result_window (default 10,000) enforces a hard ceiling. search_after uses the last document's sort values as a cursor for depth-independent sequential paging instead.

flashcards.q: Why is a cardinality aggregation approximate by default?
flashcards.a: It uses HyperLogLog++ under the hood, trading exactness for bounded memory on high-cardinality fields. precision_threshold trades more memory for tighter accuracy up to a configurable cardinality.

flashcards.q: What does the translog protect that flushed segments don't?
flashcards.a: The translog is a write-ahead log of raw operations fsync'd per request by default, protecting anything written after the last flush and before the next one -- on unclean shutdown it's replayed to recover unflushed operations.

flashcards.q: How would you diagnose why a search result's ranking looks wrong?
flashcards.a: Run the query with explain:true (or the _explain API) to get the exact per-term BM25 breakdown (term frequency, IDF, length normalization contributions) rather than guessing at relevance tuning blind.

flashcards.q: What vector search capability does modern Elasticsearch have, and its default hybrid fusion method?
flashcards.a: dense_vector fields with HNSW-based approximate kNN search (knn query clause), plus exact brute-force search when configured without HNSW. Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) is the default method for combining lexical (BM25) and vector scores in a hybrid query.

flashcards.q: When is Elasticsearch's native vector search the right call versus a dedicated vector database?
flashcards.a: Right call when you already run Elasticsearch for lexical/log search and want hybrid retrieval without new infrastructure. A dedicated vector DB wins at very large pure-vector scale with heavy filtering and multi-tenancy needs where ANN recall/latency is the primary concern.
